name: Cape Town
info: Cape Town is a port city on Table Bay at the south-western tip of Africa, founded in 1652 as a Dutch East India Company station on Khoe and San land, later a British colonial capital and today the legislative capital of South Africa.

facts.founded: Jan van Riebeeck and other employees of the Dutch East India Company landed on 6 April 1652 to establish a permanent station at the Cape; Khoe and San peoples had lived in the region long before.
facts.where: On the shore of Table Bay, at the foot of Table Mountain, on the Cape Peninsula in the Western Cape of South Africa.
facts.known: The Khoe and San peoples of the Cape; the Dutch East India Company's station of 1652; the Castle of Good Hope; slavery and its end; the Cape Qualified Franchise; District Six and the forced removals of apartheid; Robben Island; Nelson Mandela's first public speech after his release
facts.today: Cape Town is the legislative capital of South Africa, the seat of its Parliament, and the capital of the Western Cape.

t: Khoe and San peoples lived on the Cape peninsula and traded with passing ships long before the Dutch East India Company landed in 1652 and began a permanent settlement.
The Dutch and then the British ruled the city, which depended on enslaved labour until the 1830s and drew on people brought from Asia and Africa, and it passed to Britain permanently in 1814.
Under apartheid whole communities were removed, most notably the more than 60,000 residents of District Six, and the city remains one of the most racially segregated in South Africa.
dyk: In 1510 the Portuguese admiral Francisco de Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed at the Battle of Salt River by the Goringhaiqua, who used cattle trained to respond to whistles and shouts.
ev: Bartolomeu Dias reaches the Cape and names it the Cape of Storms
The Goringhaiqua defeat a Portuguese force at the Battle of Salt River

sections.origins:
Cape Town stands on the shore of Table Bay, beneath Table Mountain, on the Cape Peninsula at the south-western extremity of the African continent. The earliest known remnants of human occupation in the region were found at Peers Cave in Fish Hoek in the late 1920s; radiocarbon dates for one sample, SAM-AP 4692, fall in the mid-Holocene, at 5448 and 5136 BCE on the most generous and conservative estimates. Archaeologists have established that the peninsula and the south-western coastline were inhabited by various Khoe and San peoples, who mostly lived a semi-nomadic life. They included independent Khoe farmers with large families, the ǁAmmaqua (Watermans), a small group of Khoe traders, the Sonqua line-fishermen, a San offshoot, and the Ubiqua, a San clan of herder-hunters inland. The German anthropologist Theophilus Hahn recorded the original name of the area as ǁHui ǃGais, a Khoe word meaning "where clouds gather", and the Khoi called Table Mountain Hoeri 'kwaggo, "sea mountain".

Bartolomeu Dias arrived in 1488 and named the point the Cape of Storms; John II of Portugal later renamed it the Cape of Good Hope. Vasco da Gama recorded a sighting in 1497, and in 1503 the Portuguese admiral António de Saldanha named the mountain Taboa do Cabo, "table of the cape". In 1510 a Portuguese force led by Francisco de Almeida was defeated at the Battle of Salt River by the Goringhaiqua, a Khoekhoe clan, and Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed.
sections.growth:
Ships stopped at Table Bay long before the Dutch settled. Maritime records show that at least 1070 ships stopped at the Cape on outward-bound journeys between 1600 and 1652, and French, Danish, Dutch, English and above all Portuguese ships traded tobacco, copper and iron with the Khoikhoi clans for fresh meat and other provisions. The ǁAmmaqua supplied meat, water, salt and timber; between 1601 and 1608 they traded 1839 sheep and 149 cattle to four ships. This trade led them to build a permanent trading settlement by the Camissa river.

The Dutch East India Company's party of three vessels landed on 6 April 1652. It laid out vegetable gardens and orchards, the origin of the Company's Garden, and channelled water from the Camissa into canals. Work on the Castle of Good Hope began in 1666 and finished in 1679; it is the oldest building in South Africa. Simon van der Stel, governor from 1679, founded the Cape wine industry, and Huguenot settlers arrived in 1688. By 1754 the settlement had 5,510 Europeans and 6,729 slaves. The Cape Town Municipality was formed in 1840, with 20,016 people, of whom 10,560 were white. The first railway line opened in 1859, and between 1891 and 1901 the population more than doubled, from 67,000 to 171,000. Johannesburg overtook Cape Town as the country's largest city by the 1936 census.
sections.rulers:
The Dutch East India Company held the Cape from 1652. Its monopoly on trade barred any private trade, and it granted farms along the Liesbeek River to a few servants from 1657. In 1795, with the Netherlands invaded by France and the Company ruined, British forces took the Cape after the Battle of Muizenberg. The Cape was in Dutch hands again from 1803, and British forces occupied it once more in 1806 after the Battle of Blaauwberg. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814 ceded it permanently to the United Kingdom, which saw control of the Cape as key to its command in India.

Cape Town became the capital of the Cape Colony, whose territory expanded through the 1800s, partly through wars with the amaXhosa on its eastern frontier. The Cape Town Legislative Council was established in 1834. The colony elected its first parliament in 1854 on the non-racial Cape Qualified Franchise and won responsible government, with its own prime minister, in 1872. Cecil Rhodes, as prime minister, later restricted that franchise. In 1910 the Union of South Africa made Cape Town the legislative capital. After the National Party's victory in 1948 the already limited voting rights of the Coloured community in Cape Province were revoked. The first democratic election took place on 27 April 1994.
sections.life:
The Dutch gave their own names to the people they met, calling the pastoralists "Hottentots", the coastal shellfish-eaters "Strandlopers" and the hunter-gatherers "Bushmen". The first Asian immigrants, from 1654, were banished to the Cape by the Batavian High Court; they helped to form the Cape Coloured and Cape Malay communities and brought Islam to the Cape. In 1658 the first large group of 402 enslaved people was brought to work the farms, from present-day Benin and Angola, and from then on non-European migrants outnumbered Europeans. Enslaved people were also imported from Indonesia and Madagascar, and trading in slaves remained significant; in 1766 the enslaved people on the slaver Meermin mutinied. When slavery ended in the 1830s, over 5500 enslaved people in the city were freed, almost a third of its population, and a Muslim community went on to found the Bo-Kaap.

After 1806 the native inhabitants were made to declare a fixed residence and could not move between regions without written permission; the vagrancy and pass laws of 1809 were repealed in 1829. Before the middle of the 20th century Cape Town was one of the most racially integrated cities in South Africa. In the 2011 census 35.7% of the metropolitan municipality's residents spoke Afrikaans as a first language, 29.8% Xhosa and 28.4% English. The dish bobotie dates from the 17th century, and the Kaapse Klopse minstrel carnival is held each year on 2 January.
sections.crises:
The first of the border conflicts between the Company's settlement and the Khoekhoe began in 1659 to 1660, when Nommoa, also known as Doman, organised resistance among several Khoekhoe groups after Van Riebeeck granted farms along the Liesbeek, grazing land of the Khoe. The Convict Crisis of 1849 followed a British proposal to make the Cape a penal colony and brought substantial civil upheaval.

Segregation first appeared after an outbreak of bubonic plague that was blamed on native Africans, who were moved to two locations outside the city, one near the docks and one at Ndabeni, about six km east. Ndabeni began what later grew into the townships of the Cape Flats. Under apartheid the Group Areas Act of 1950 classified and segregated urban areas by race, and formerly multiracial suburbs were purged of residents or demolished. District Six was declared a whites-only area in 1965; all its housing was demolished and over 60,000 residents were forcibly removed, many to the Cape Flats. Black South Africans were expelled to Langa, the city's oldest township, and the Cape was made a "Coloured labour preference area", to the exclusion of Black Africans. The government tried for decades to remove the largely Xhosa squatter camps such as Crossroads, and in the last forced removal, in May and June 1986, an estimated 70,000 people were expelled from their homes. In June 1976 school students in Langa, Gugulethu and Nyanga held their own protests after the Soweto Uprising; school buildings were burnt and the police met them with force.
sections.legacy:
Several old places remain: the Castle of Good Hope, the oldest building in South Africa, and the Company's Garden, the country's oldest park. Robben Island in Table Bay, a place of banishment and imprisonment for nearly 400 years and also a leper colony and a mental hospital, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999. Nelson Mandela served 18 of his 27 years of imprisonment there, as did Kgalema Motlanthe and Jacob Zuma. On 11 February 1990, hours after his release, Mandela spoke from the balcony of the City Hall in his first public speech in decades. The District Six Museum records the history of the Cape Coloured community and of District Six.

Cape Town is the legislative capital of South Africa and the seat of its Parliament, the capital of the Western Cape and the country's second-most populous city. The 2011 census counted 3,740,026 people in the metropolitan municipality. Table Mountain National Park lies within the city boundaries, in the Cape Floristic Region. About 60% of the population live in townships and informal settlements far from the centre, and the legacy of apartheid's planning means that Cape Town remains one of the most racially segregated cities in South Africa.

summary: Cape Town was inhabited by Khoe and San peoples before the Dutch East India Company founded a station there in 1652. Enslaved and banished people were brought to it, Britain took it permanently in 1814, and apartheid removed whole districts such as District Six. It is South Africa's legislative capital.
notes: START 1652: the formal colonisation and the city's founding as the articles give it; Khoe and San occupation is much earlier and is told in the origins section.

CONFLICT, District Six: the main article says it was declared whites-only in 1965 and that all housing was then demolished; the history article says it was bulldozed and declared white-only in 1966. I used 1965 and the main article's wording.

CONFLICT, return of the Cape to the Dutch: the main article says by treaty in 1803, the history article says 1802 under a peace agreement, with the Cape under Dutch rule 1803 to 1806. I used 1803 only as the history article's rule dates, and gave no treaty year.

CONFLICT, abolition of slavery: the main article says 1833, freeing over 5500 slaves in the city; the history article says emancipation in 1834 and estimates about 39,000 slaves (colony-wide, implied). I wrote 'in the 1830s' and kept the city figure of over 5500 from the main article. The Cape Town Legislative Council 1834 is from the history article.

ORIGIN of the enslaved: the history article gives the 402 as from present-day Benin and Angola; the main article says the labour shortage prompted the import of enslaved people from Indonesia and Madagascar. Both are given, not as a contradiction. The history article says 'the first large contingent' in 1658 'in the following year' after 1657; I used 1658.
ABOLITION: 'Rhodes ... restricted the multiracial franchise' is from the history article; its date is not given.
The plague segregation and Ndabeni: the history article gives no year ('This period'); left undated.
The history article says the Cape was 'under Dutch rule from 1652 to 1795 and again from 1803 to 1806'; I used this. The Battle of Muizenberg is named without a date, as in the article.

DISPLACEMENT of Khoe and San after 1652 beyond the 1659-60 conflict, the Khoekhoe's later fate, the Cape Coloured people's origins beyond the articles' statements, and the Group Areas Act's wider effects are not detailed in either article and were left out. No population figure for the Khoekhoe or San is given.

The history article says the Dutch 'bartered with the native Khoisan for their sheep and cattle'; I did not include how the land passed to the settlers because neither article says more than the farm grants.
Quotation marks around 'Hottentots', 'Strandlopers', 'Bushmen' are the articles' own, as the Dutch names; they are named as the Dutch usage.

Population 3,740,026 is the 2011 census figure of the metropolitan municipality; the article also gives 4,004,793 for a 2016 community survey. 'About 60% live in townships and informal settlements' is the article's undated claim.
Peers Cave dating: the article says earlier estimates of an upper Pleistocene origin were revised; I gave only the revised Holocene dates.
Left out: tourism, rankings, governance and budget, climate, flora, sport, transport, the water crisis of 2015 to 2018 and the 2021 taxi violence.
